newsitem.title: THAILAND: Bold steps only beginning to restore Thai economy.
newsitem.headline: Bold steps only beginning to restore Thai economy.

text.p: Thailand's economy is seen mired in problems for some time despite strong medicine administered by the government, analysts said on Thursday.

Measures taken by the authorities since last week to force mergers of 16 ailing finance companies with healthy ones and a stunning move to float the embattled baht would help cure some sectors, the analysts said.
But more bitter medication was needed in the form of lower interest rates, increased liquidity to help businesses, cutting debt and streamlining regulations on foreign investment, the analysts said.

"The latest steps taken are good and like a tank of oxygen. Unless more significant changes are made in the next two to three months, this tank of oxygen could be used up and Thailand could be in a worse position," said Kenneth Courtis, chief economist at Deutsche Bank Group Asia Pacific.

Thai authorities acted decisively as the economy sputtered to its worst slump in over a decade. Its finance sector is saddled with billions of dollars in non-performing loans to the cash-strapped property sector, the stock market has fallen to eight year lows and the baht was a target of speculators.
Official estimates of 1997 Thai economic growth are 5.6 percent, despite looming fiscal 1997 and 1998 budget deficit forecasts, the first such shortfalls in more than a decade.
But private economists put growth at between three and five percent against 6.4 percent in 1996.
Courtis saw the economy growing 3.0-3.5 percent while Sriyan Pietersz, strategist at Capital Nomura Securities, expected it to grow at around 3.7 percent.
The forced mergers and the baht's flotation were cheered by foreign investors. The stock market leapt sharply this week as foreign buying returned but the baht plummeted to record lows offshore.

"The authorities have done quite a bit already but I see a need to bring down interest rates quickly to inject more liquidity into the system and stimulate the economy to take the stress off it," said Pietersz.

Other analysts said Thai economic problems would linger into next year despite short term fixes because unwinding finance firm woes, seeing their forced mergers through or arranging suitable partners for them could be drawn-out tasks.
A foreign banker who declined to be identified said there was little experience in mergers in Thailand and the process could take many months to complete for many firms.
The expected delay would weigh on the tottering economy while other measures such as the much-vaunted securitisation of Thai property loans had not progressed.

Bank of Thailand Governor Rerngchai Marakanond said late on Wednesday that with the floating of the baht, the central bank would not have to be wary about defending the currency and could be more flexible in its high rates policy and see more inflows.
"In the past not only did inflows decrease, there were also a lot of outflows causing liquidity problems," he said.
Analysts, however, do not see rates coming down soon, especially after the central bank raised its discount rate to 12.5 percent from 10.5 after the baht float.
Many believe the baht flotation will help the sluggish exports sector, curb imports of expensive luxuries and reduce overseas travel by Thais.

But the already wide current account deficit was seen ballooning as the cheaper baht raised import bills. Foreign debt rose almost immediately by about 20 percent in line with the baht's depreciation following the float, analysts said.

Thai Rating and Information Services, the rating agency, said total outstanding Thai debt at end-1996 was $16.8 billion for the government, $13.9 billion for state enterprises and $62.3 billion for the private sector.
Former finance minister Surakiart Sathirathai said he saw most of the economic maladies being cleared away within a year as a result of the tough measures being taken.
"I see light at the end of the tunnel within one year," said Surakiart, who is an economic adviser to the prime minister.
